teaser: A winged genius sits surrounded by tools and does nothing. Dürer hid the reason in plain sight.
review_notes:
Dürer's diary of the Netherlands journey (1520-21) records giving away 'a Melancholy' together with 'a Jerome'; the lesson says he often handed them out as a pair.
Dürer's note on a preparatory sketch: 'key means power, purse means wealth'.
Dürer's mother Barbara died in May 1514; any link to the print is presented as a guess, not a fact.
The reading of the 'I' via Agrippa's three kinds of melancholy (Panofsky) is presented as one proposal.
Sheet size about 24 x 19 cm.
Claim that his wife Agnes sold his prints at fairs.
The 4 and 1 beside the date read as D and A is a popular observation, presented as such.

lesson.text: This picture was never meant for a wall. No church ordered it, no prince, no chapel. It was made for a table: for a pair of hands, good daylight, and a person willing to sit with it for an hour. The sheet is about 24 by 19 cm (roughly 9.5 by 7.5 inches), smaller than a page of printer paper.

It is an engraving. Albrecht Dürer cut every line into a copper plate with a burin, a small steel blade pushed by the palm. Ink was rubbed into the grooves, damp paper was laid on top, and a press squeezed the two together. One plate could give hundreds of sheets, each one light enough to travel across Europe in a merchant's bag.

Dürer had no gallery. His wife Agnes sold his prints from a stall at markets and fairs, and he carried stacks of them on his travels to trade or give away. In his travel diary he notes handing this print out together with another one, his Saint Jerome, as a pair.

So what did the buyer find on the table? A heavy, winged woman sitting on a step, in Nuremberg, in 1514. Around her lies enough equipment to build a house or measure the sky. None of it is in use. Start with her, and with the two companions who share her corner.

lesson.title: Three ways of sitting still
lesson.text: Everyone in this picture is seated or lying down. Follow them one by one.

spots.title: The stare
spots.text: Her cheek rests on her fist, an old sign of gloom. The face is in deep shadow, but the eyes are bright and wide open. She is not asleep or bored. She is thinking hard about something she cannot reach.

spots.title: The idle compass
spots.text: Her other hand holds a compass, the tool for drawing circles and taking measurements. She grips it loosely, pointing at nothing. A closed book sits under her arm.

spots.title: The busy child
spots.text: A small winged boy perches on a millstone and scribbles on a tablet. He is the only one working, and he does it without a thought. Doing is easy when you do not ask why.

spots.title: The dog
spots.text: A thin dog is curled up tight, ribs showing. Dogs were thought to share their master's mood, so this one sleeps through the scene, hungry and worn out.

lesson.text: The title gives the diagnosis. In Dürer's day doctors believed the body held four fluids, called humors, and that your character depended on which one ruled. Too much black bile made you melancholic: slow, sad, lonely, the unluckiest of the four types.

Around 1500, scholars in Italy turned the old idea upside down: the gloomy temperament was also the temperament of thinkers and artists. Dürer's figure has wings and a wreath because her sadness is the price of a brilliant mind.

That explains the mess on the floor. A plane, a saw, nails, a ruler, a ball, a huge cut stone: the tools of carpenters, builders and geometers. For Dürer, measuring was the root of all art. Yet measuring only goes so far, and she seems to have hit the limit. On the wall behind her hangs one more instrument of numbers. It hides a message.
Dürer wrote the year he made this print inside the picture, as two numbers side by side in a grid. Can you spot them?

spots.title: 15 and 14
spots.text: The two middle boxes of the bottom row read 15 and 14: the year 1514. Dürer had to build the whole number grid around that pair, which is far harder than it looks.

lesson.text: The grid is a magic square. Add the four numbers in any row, any column or either diagonal and you get 34. The four corners give 34 too, and so do the four boxes in the middle. People have also noticed that the 4 and the 1 beside the date match D and A, the fourth and first letters of the alphabet: Dürer, Albrecht.

1514 was a hard year for him. His mother, Barbara, died that May after a long illness. He had drawn her in charcoal two months earlier, gaunt and wide-eyed, and he wrote down an account of her last hours. Some people read this print as mourning. He never said so.

Then there is the stone. It is a block with its corners sliced off, and nobody is sure what to call it or why it is there. Mathematicians still argue over its exact angles. Some viewers see a faint face or skull in the stains on its front side. It may simply be the hardest shape Dürer could think of to draw in perspective, the art of making flat things look deep.

The sky is no calmer. A comet or star blazes over the sea under a rainbow, and a bat-like creature carries the title on its skin. As for the “I” after the word, one proposal is that a German book of the time listed three levels of melancholy, and the first belonged to people ruled by imagination: artists.

spots.title: The title bearer
spots.text: A small beast with a bat's wings and a snake's tail holds up the word MELENCOLIA and the mysterious I. Bats fly at dusk, the hour linked to this mood.

spots.title: The blazing star
spots.text: Rays shoot out in every direction, each one a single straight cut in the copper. A rainbow curves above it. Comets were read as warnings, rainbows as promises: the sky gives both at once.

spots.title: The puzzle stone
spots.text: Eight faces, sharp edges, one tip pointing up. The shading is built from thousands of tiny dots and dashes. Search the large front face for the pale ghost of a head.

spots.title: The hourglass
spots.text: The sand has run about halfway. A small sundial sits on top of the frame. Time is passing while she sits.

spots.title: The scales
spots.text: A balance hangs from the wall, perfectly level and perfectly empty. Like the bell beside the number square, it is ready and unused.

spots.title: Keys at her belt
spots.text: A bunch of keys dangles from her belt, and a purse lies crumpled near her feet. On a sketch for the print Dürer wrote his own short gloss: the key means power, the purse means wealth.

spots.title: Tools on the floor
spots.text: A carpenter's plane, a saw, a ruler and a few nails lie where they were dropped. These are tools for making real things, set aside.

spots.title: The signature
spots.text: On the side of the step: 1514 and the monogram, a D tucked under the legs of a large A. Dürer's mark was so valuable that other printmakers forged it.

lesson.text: This sheet is one of three large engravings Dürer made in 1513 and 1514, all nearly the same size, that collectors later nicknamed his “master engravings”. The other two show a knight on horseback and a saint writing in a sunny study. Dürer never called them a set.

Five centuries of scholars have written about this small piece of paper, more than about almost any other print. No reading has won. Perhaps that is the design: a picture about a mind that cannot finish its thought, built so that yours cannot finish either. What do you think she is waiting for?

quiz.question: How was this picture made?
options: Painted in oil on a wooden panel
Cut into a copper plate, inked and printed on paper
quiz.explanation: It is an engraving: lines cut in copper with a burin, then printed.

quiz.question: What do the rows, columns and diagonals of the number square add up to?
quiz.explanation: Every row, column and diagonal of the magic square gives 34.

quiz.question: Who is the only figure actually working?
options: The small winged boy on the millstone
quiz.explanation: The child scribbles on his tablet while the woman sits idle.

quiz.question: What new idea about melancholy does the print reflect?
options: That it could be cured by music
That it was the temperament of thinkers and artists
That it only affected old people
quiz.explanation: Scholars around 1500 linked the gloomy temperament to creative genius.

quiz.question: Where did Dürer hide the year 1514?
options: In the bottom row of the number square
quiz.explanation: The two middle boxes of the bottom row read 15 and 14.

facts.text: Melencolia I was ordered by a church for its altar.
facts.explanation: Nobody commissioned it: it was a print sold and given away on loose sheets.

facts.text: The winged woman holds a compass but is not using it.
facts.explanation: She grips it loosely in her lap, pointing at nothing.

facts.text: Scholars agree on what the cut stone block means.
facts.explanation: Its shape and meaning are still debated.
